source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: A training of under one hour on probabilistic reasoning (including comparison classes and base rates) made forecasters more accurate in all four tournament years, in a randomized design.
numbers: Year 1: probability-trained n=119 mean standardized Brier -0.05, scenario-trained n=113 -0.06, control n=152 +0.07, F(2,381)=12.1, p<.001; about 10% and 11% Brier improvement. Year 2: trained n=205 -0.10 vs control n=194 +0.05, t(395)=5.95, 12% improvement. Year 3 about 6%, year 4 about 7%.
limits: Training bundled comparison classes with averaging, models, bias awareness and belief updating (CHAMP), so the effect is not the outside view alone. Gain shrank after year 2. Standardized Brier is within question.
agent_relevance: Outside view is one part of a cheap bundle; expect single-digit to low-teens percent Brier gains, not a large one.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Among trained forecasters who tagged their own explanations, the comparison-classes tag had the best accuracy of all ten principles.
numbers: Standardized (within-question) mean Brier: comparison classes 0.17 (n=580 explanations); math/statistical models 0.26 (n=453); select right questions 0.26 (n=330); hunt for information 0.38 (n=2,992); update/adjust 0.44 (n=1,239); post-mortem 1.04 (n=88); control explanations 0.49 (n=6,622). ANOVA for C: F=12.28, p<.001.
limits: The 0.17 is a standardized score (deviation from the question mean), NOT a raw Brier score. Tags were self-reported by forecasters after the fact and tag use is not randomized, so question type and forecaster skill are confounded. Year-4 analysis only. Reading it as 'outside view lowers Brier from 0.26 to 0.17' is a misreading.
agent_relevance: The S0 line in SUBFIELDS.md should say standardized and correlational. Direction is plausible; size is not a usable effect size.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Authors say the C principle was the largest contributor, but warn the others may matter too, since the package was designed to work together.
numbers: Probabilistic-reasoning principles (C,H,A,M,S) were associated with better accuracy; political-reasoning principles (KNOW) were not. Post-mortem (P) and other-perspectives (O) tags were linked to worse scores (P 1.04, O 0.63), likely because they are written after errors or on hard questions.
limits: Reverse causation: forecasters invoke some principles because the question is already going badly. The same bias could inflate or deflate the C tag.
agent_relevance: Do not read tag-level scores as causal. A check of tag use against question difficulty is needed before gating S0 on this number.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Moderators: cognitive ability and concentrated practice predicted accuracy; training did not interact with individual differences.
numbers: Hypotheses H4 to H6 (training x ability, motivation, practice interactions) unsupported. Numeracy and spatial reasoning were not predictive. Practice (forecasts per question) mediated the training effect in 3 of 4 years. Prior-year experience alone did not improve Brier. Trained and control spent similar time (4.1 vs 3.7 hours per week).
limits: Self-selected volunteers with high education; forecasters could choose questions. Training included score feedback.
agent_relevance: The outside-view benefit looks general across ability levels, so a scaffold step should help weaker and stronger reasoners alike. Depth per question beats breadth.

source: AI Impacts (2019, updated) Evidence on good forecasting practices from the Good Judgment Project
finding: The secondary source behind our S0 line. It reports comparison-class tag Brier 0.17 vs 0.26 for the next best, citing Chang et al. 2016.
numbers: Reports 0.17 vs 0.26 as average Brier. Lists use of the outside view 12th of 15 correlates of success. No sample sizes, confidence intervals or tests given.
limits: Page says correlations only, mainly geopolitical short-horizon questions. Read through a fetch summary, not raw HTML. It drops the 'standardized' qualifier found in the primary (see b02).
agent_relevance: Cite the primary (b02), not this page. Our 0.17 vs 0.26 line needs the word standardized.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right
finding: Founding applied case for reference class forecasting: build a distribution of outcomes from past similar projects, place the project in it, and uplift the budget to the risk level you accept.
numbers: Cost overrun in constant prices: rail 44.7% average, bridges and tunnels 33.8%, roads 20.4%, no improvement over 70 years. Road class: 172 projects; uplift 15% at 50% overrun risk, 32% at 20% risk, 45% at 10% risk. Rail uplift 40% at 50% risk, 57% at 20% risk, 68% at 10% risk.
limits: Paper presents the method and the distributions. It gives no out-of-sample test of accuracy gain from using the uplifts; first use recorded Oct 2004 by the UK Department for Transport.
agent_relevance: The method needs a class with outcome data. Without a number-bearing class the step degrades to a guess. Choosing a quantile of the class, not the mean, is reusable.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right
finding: Stated boundary condition: the outside view helps most on non-routine projects; choosing the class gets harder for new technologies.
numbers: Rail passenger forecasts wrong by average 51.4% (84% of rail projects off by more than 20%); road traffic average 9.5% error, half off by more than 20%.
limits: Author is an advocate; the claim that most projects are non-routine locally yet use known technology is asserted, not tested.
agent_relevance: The class-choice step is the weak point. Agent should record which class was picked and a second-best class.

source: Lovallo and Kahneman (2003) Delusions of success, as reported in Flyvbjerg (2006)
finding: Reported experiment: incoming students rated future performance. A group first asked for entrance scores and peer scores cut its expected rating by about 20%.
numbers: First group expected to beat 84% of peers (logically impossible). Outside-view diversion lowered the second group's rating by 20%, still overconfident.
limits: Seen only as quoted in Flyvbjerg. No N, design or test statistic read. Unverified until the primary is opened.
agent_relevance: A short prompt to recall the distribution before judging reduces optimism but does not remove it.

source: Buehler, Griffin, Ross (1994) Exploring the planning fallacy, as reported in Thomas and Koenig (2018)
finding: Founding planning fallacy result: people predicting their own task times focus on the plan; prompting them to recall past task performance just before predicting reduced the underestimate.
numbers: Not read in primary. Thomas and Koenig report only the direction.
limits: Secondhand. No effect size.
agent_relevance: Supports a recall-past-cases-first prompt, but exact gain unknown.

source: Thomas and Koenig (2018) Knowledge of previous tasks: task similarity influences bias in task duration predictions
finding: Three experiments: predictions on the second task were less biased when the first task was the same task. Being told the earlier duration did not change bias.
numbers: Exp 1 n=40. Essay-first group predicted 33.40 min vs actual 30.11 (slight overestimate); castle-first group predicted 19.70 vs actual 38.14 (large underestimate). Duration feedback had no effect on bias in all three experiments.
limits: Student sample, small lab tasks, one week gap. Exps 2 and 3 sample sizes not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Giving the base rate is not enough; it must come from a class that matches the target. A dissimilar class gives little help and may mislead.

source: Benjamin et al. (2022) Principal investigators over-optimistically forecast scientific and operational outcomes for clinical trials
finding: Experts forecasting their own projects (inside view) were no better than a 50% guess on trial success and worse on recruitment and timelines.
numbers: 740 PIs (16.7% response). Brier: primary outcome 0.25 (CI 0.20-0.30), recruitment 0.38 (0.33-0.42), timeline 0.52 (0.50-0.55). AUC 0.76, 0.64, 0.55. Calibration index 0.064, 0.150, 0.406. Predictions exceeded observed frequencies.
limits: Low response rate; compared with uninformative 50%, not with a base-rate forecast from similar trials, so it does not test the outside view directly.
agent_relevance: Shows the cost of the inside view in a high-stakes domain; a base-rate forecast is a natural baseline to beat.

source: Bruckmaier et al. (2021) Tversky and Kahneman's cognitive illusions: who can solve them, and why?
finding: Large school sample treating Bayesian reasoning, Linda and Wason tasks as a group; asks if they are one skill and whether they differ from intelligence and maths.
numbers: N=2,643 Luxembourg students aged 16-18. Cites earlier work: natural-frequency versions solved far more often than probability versions (about 24% vs 4% in one cited case).
limits: I read the abstract and introduction, not the regression results. School students, not experts.
agent_relevance: Base-rate use is a skill that varies between people; for a model, the format of the information may matter more than ability.

source: Boosting for insight and/or boosting for agency? How to maximize accurate test interpretation with natural frequencies (2023) BMC Med Educ
finding: Presenting base-rate information as natural frequencies doubled correct Bayesian answers; a short training raised it further.
numbers: 577 medical students, pre/post. Conditional probabilities 34% correct; natural frequencies without training 68%; probabilities after training 64%; natural frequencies after training 89%.
limits: Medical students on diagnostic tasks with given numbers; not forecasting with self-built classes.
agent_relevance: If the agent writes the base rate, write it as counts (7 of 100) before combining it with case evidence.

source: Preregistered randomized crossover trial of odds and likelihood ratios vs natural frequencies (2025) BMC Med Educ
finding: Natural frequencies beat odds/likelihood ratios for a single test, but both fail often when two pieces of evidence must be chained.
numbers: 167 medical and 162 psychology students. Single-test PPV correct: natural frequencies 36.2% vs odds/LR 21.6% (OR 2.41). Two sequential tests: odds/LR 10.6% vs natural frequencies 4.9% (OR 2.73).
limits: Student sample; correct-answer rates low even in the best format.
agent_relevance: Chaining several adjustments from a base rate is where humans fail. Do the adjustment arithmetic in code, not in the model's text.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Their best retrieval-and-reasoning system uses a scratchpad prompt that asks for historical base rates and an over/under-confidence check. The prompt itself added little.
numbers: Full system Brier .179 vs human crowd .149 (accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%). Without fine-tuning .186. Without fine-tuning and retrieval .206, equal to best zero-shot baseline .208 (GPT-4-1106). The paper calls the reasoning prompt's gain 'fairly minor'.
limits: Base-rate instruction was bundled with other prompt parts, so no isolated outside-view ablation. Questions are 2023-24 platform questions.
agent_relevance: A base-rate sentence in a prompt gives a small gain; retrieval of facts gave the large one.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: System is best where the crowd is unsure and worst where the crowd is confident.
numbers: Crowd predictions 0.3-0.7: system Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Where the crowd is near 0 or 1 the crowd wins. Averaging system and crowd gave the best score. Performance approached the crowd only with at least 5 relevant retrieved articles.
limits: Selective-setting results used validation-based tuning; fine-tuning set was 13,253 samples.
agent_relevance: Where the base rate is already extreme, the crowd's anchor wins; the model should not push far from a strong base rate.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Benchmark baselines include a prompt that makes the model name a reference class and base rate first, then adjust up and down. Models did not match superforecasters.
numbers: Brier on the 200-question human subset: superforecasters 0.096, general public 0.121, best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122. Best LLM without crowd forecast on market questions 0.136. With combination questions: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. Gap to superforecasters 0.054 vs 0.026 between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Top LLMs saw the crowd forecast as a freeze value, itself a strong base rate. No ablation of the reference-class step.
agent_relevance: Giving the model a good anchor (crowd value) helped most; same logic as an outside view, but from data, not recall.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Brier score falls roughly log-linearly with training compute; extrapolated parity with superforecasters is far off and uncertain.
numbers: Log-linear fit r=-0.67, p=0.046; parity at about 6.49e26 FLOP, bootstrapped 95% CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28.
limits: Nine-ish models, marginal significance, extrapolation.
agent_relevance: Model strength still dominates prompt tricks; do not expect an outside-view step to close the gap alone.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Largest direct test of a base-rate prompt on LLMs. Study 1: 38 prompts on 4 models, 100 ForecastBench questions. 'Base Rate First' gave a small gain in simple tests that disappeared in the preregistered mixed model.
numbers: Base Rate First: mean Brier difference vs control -0.016 (SD 0.106, N=390), adj p=.036 by t-test; mixed model estimate -0.011, adj p=.774. Frequency-Based Reasoning -0.019 (N=370), adj p=.022; mixed model adj p=.774. Mean Brier across prompts: GPT-4o 0.215, Sonnet 0.208, Haiku 0.214, Llama 405B 0.227.
quote: Before considering the specific details of this question, what is the historical frequency of similar events?
limits: 100 questions; gains about 0.01-0.02 Brier, same order as differences between prompts. Base Rate First text asks for the historical frequency of similar events, then adjust.
agent_relevance: Base-rate-first prompts are weakly positive at best on frontier LLMs. Run our own A/B before fixing it in S0.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Study 1: telling the model to reason as a Bayesian made forecasts worse; so did Propose-Evaluate-Select.
numbers: Bayesian Reasoning: mean Brier +0.025 (SD 0.172, N=388), adj p=.036; mixed model +0.03, p<.001. Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.028 (N=391), adj p=.010, worse in the mixed model too. Both made forecasts more decisive (17.2-19.9 points from 50%) than control (about 13 points).
limits: Mechanism (overconfidence from decisive forecasts) is inferred, not tested.
agent_relevance: Asking for explicit Bayes updating invites overconfident, wrong numbers; keep updates small and computed by code.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt engineering large language models' forecasting capabilities
finding: Study 2: compound prompts combining base rates with chain of thought, pros and cons, etc. gave no reliable gain on 5 models including o1 and o1-mini. A superforecaster-authored odds-ratio prompt was worse.
numbers: Brier by model: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 405B 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Sonnet 0.207. Base Rate First + Chain of Thought: 0.000, adj p=.985. All Human prompt (base rate + pros and cons): -0.009, adj p=.985. Superforecaster Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt: +0.023, z=4.165, adj p=.01 (worse). Base Rate First + Frequency prompt mean forecast 38.4%.
limits: About 1,700-1,900 forecasts per model; some refusals. 100 questions only.
agent_relevance: Stacking human-derived tricks did not add up; the compound outside-view prompt is not better than a plain call. Argues for measuring, not assuming.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: A base-rate-neglecting, overconfident assistant still raised human accuracy about as much as a good one, so outside-view advice is not what carries the gain.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Superforecasting assistant (prompted to start from reference classes and base rates) improved accuracy 24-28% vs control; without one outlier item 41% vs 29% for the noisy base-rate-neglecting assistant.
limits: Control had a weaker model without numbers, so the gain may come from any numeric anchor. Outlier item drives part of the result.
agent_relevance: Any concrete numeric anchor helped humans; this does not isolate the outside view.

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large language model prediction capabilities: evidence from a real-world forecasting tournament
finding: Early test: GPT-4 prompted with comparison classes and base rates did not beat the human crowd.
numbers: GPT-4 mean Brier .20 (SD .18), human crowd lower; tested against the 0.25 no-information baseline. No ablation of the base-rate sentence.
limits: Prompt combined superforecaster persona, comparison classes, base rates. Effects cannot be separated. Small question set.
agent_relevance: A prompt line alone has not shown accuracy gain in any LLM study so far.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: LLMs show an acquiescence tilt above 50% even with a long prompt that asks for reference classes first, which is a base-rate failure.
numbers: 12-LLM ensemble vs 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions: not statistically different from the human crowd. Mean model predictions significantly above 50% though outcomes nearly even. Exposure to the human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17-28%.
limits: Only 31 questions. Base-rate instruction present in the prompt in all conditions, so no comparison without it.
agent_relevance: Check the agent's mean forecast against the known share of YES in similar questions. A cheap calibration check.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) Reasoning and tools for human-level forecasting
finding: Agent transcripts show the model's first step is 'Reference classes and base rates', then it uses vague recalled numbers.
numbers: Example: Ethereum above $3700; base rate set at 30% by recalling the 2021 bull market, then averaged with 35% and 40% to a final number. No Brier effect isolated for this step.
limits: Example transcript, not a measured result. I did not extract the paper's ablation tables.
agent_relevance: LLM base rates are often vague recollections, not computed frequencies. Require a count or a source.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: Frontier model o3 on 464 Metaculus questions beat the human crowd but not expert forecasters. Its own reasoning uses reference class then adjusts.
numbers: o3 Brier 0.1352 vs human crowd 0.149; o3-pro 0.1307 on the hold-out set. Expert forecaster results: n=157 mean 0.1573, median 0.0225; hold-out n=41 mean 0.1222, median 0.0196.
limits: Prompt asked for reference classes, no ablation. Single author, preprint. Expert subset differs from the bot question set.
agent_relevance: Modern reasoning models already use the outside-view pattern unprompted, so the added value of an explicit step is unknown.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Their data builder uses reference class spanning: variants of a question with changed entities, to avoid a bias toward events that happened.
numbers: 2,621 ground-truth resolved questions, ground-truth error below 5% via Perplexity checks. Also 2,028 synthetic consistency-check questions.
limits: Used for dataset building, not a test of outside-view prompting.
agent_relevance: Models can be checked for coherence across a reference class (same question, other entities); gives a test of outside-view use.

source: Bench to the Future (2025) pastcasting benchmark
finding: Benchmark builds an offline corpus covering multiple base rates per question; prompt tells the model to lean on the inside view when no good base rate exists.
numbers: About 20,000 pages per question in the offline corpus. Prompt: base rate is a good start for regular events, put more weight on the inside view for unique ones.
limits: Describes the benchmark; I did not extract per-prompt results.
agent_relevance: Matches the boundary condition: no usable class, then shift weight to case evidence.
